children.label: b
children.prompt: Use the result from part a to complete the following.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Write the coordinates of the turning point of the path of the spacecraft.

answer.worked: In $y=3(x+1)^2-10$, the squared term is zero when $x=-1$. The minimum value is then $y=-10$, so the turning point is $(-1,-10)$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Find the exact coordinates of where the path of the spacecraft cuts the $x$-axis, leaving your answer in surd form.

answer.worked:
At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}3(x+1)^2-10&=0\\3(x+1)^2&=10\\(x+1)^2&=\frac{10}{3}\\x+1&=\pm\sqrt{\frac{10}{3}}\\x&=-1\pm\frac{\sqrt{30}}3\end{align*}$$
The intercepts are $\left(-1-\frac{\sqrt{30}}3,0\right)$ and $\left(-1+\frac{\sqrt{30}}3,0\right)$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Sketch a graph showing the path of the spacecraft and the position of the space station, $P$. Label the turning point and the $x$- and $y$-intercepts for the path of the spacecraft.

answer.short: Upward-opening parabola with turning point $(-1,-10)$, $y$-intercept $(0,-7)$ and $x$-intercepts $\left(-1\pm\frac{\sqrt{30}}3,0\right)$; mark $P(-1,-12)$.
answer.worked: From part b, the turning point is $(-1,-10)$ and the $x$-intercepts are $\left(-1\pm\frac{\sqrt{30}}3,0\right)$. When $x=0$, $y=-7$, so the $y$-intercept is $(0,-7)$. Draw an upward-opening parabola symmetric about $x=-1$, and mark $P(-1,-12)$ below its turning point.

children.label: d
children.prompt: If one unit represents 100 km, find the distance between the spacecraft and the space station when they are closest to each other.

answer.short:
$200\text{ km}$.

The closest point is the turning point directly above $P$.
answer.worked:
The path has $y\geq-10$, while the station is at $P(-1,-12)$. Every point on the path is therefore at least 2 units above the station. The turning point $(-1,-10)$ has the same $x$-coordinate as $P$, so it attains this minimum distance.
$$\begin{align*}d&=(-10)-(-12)\\d&=2\text{ units}\\d&=2\times100\text{ km}\\d&=200\text{ km}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Show that the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points of the paths of the two spacecraft can be found by solving $3x^2+x-10=0$.

answer.worked:
At an intersection, both paths have the same $x$- and $y$-coordinates. Equate their expressions for $y$:
$$\begin{align*}3x^2+6x-7&=5x+3\\3x^2+6x-7-5x-3&=0\\3x^2+x-10&=0\end{align*}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: Solve the equation in part e and hence state the coordinates of the intersection points of the paths of the two spacecraft.

answer.short: $x=-2$ or $x=\frac53$; the intersection points are $(-2,-7)$ and $\left(\frac53,\frac{34}{3}\right)$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}3x^2+x-10&=0\\(3x-5)(x+2)&=0\end{align*}$$
By the null factor law, $x=\frac53$ or $x=-2$.

When $x=\frac53$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=5\left(\frac53\right)+3\\y&=\frac{25}{3}+\frac93\\y&=\frac{34}{3}\end{align*}$$
When $x=-2$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=5(-2)+3\\y&=-7\end{align*}$$
The intersection points are $\left(\frac53,\frac{34}{3}\right)$ and $(-2,-7)$.
